identity.title: The Complexity of Two-Team Polymatrix Games with Independent Adversaries

problem.claim: The paper studies computing Nash equilibria in polymatrix games with pairwise zero-sum or coordination interactions, especially when players form a small number of identical-interest teams.

gap.claim: Although the three-team case is known to be PPAD-complete, the complexity of the two-team case had remained open.

contributions.claim: Proves that computing equilibria in the two-team version is CLS-hard.
Shows the lower bound is tight when one team contains multiple independent adversaries.
Proves hardness of finding any stationary point for a class of bilinear polynomial objectives in the simplest stated non-convex-concave min-max constrained setting.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors identify CLS-hardness for the previously open two-team version and report tightness in the independent-adversary setting.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report a CLS-hardness result for the two-team equilibrium-computation problem.
The authors report that this lower bound is tight when one team consists of multiple independent adversaries.
The authors report stationary-point hardness for a class of bilinear polynomial min-max objectives.

narrative_sequence.summary: Polymatrix zero-sum games provide a multiplayer setting with efficiently computable Nash equilibria.
The study extends attention to pairwise zero-sum-or-coordination games with players grouped into identical-interest teams.
The three-team case is known to be PPAD-complete, while the two-team complexity was open.
The paper reports CLS-hardness for two teams and tightness when one team has multiple independent adversaries.
A related route establishes stationary-point hardness for a bilinear polynomial min-max class.

source_observation.claim: The abstract moves from a known tractable case and an open complexity boundary to a precise hardness classification, then states the condition under which the bound is tight.

lessons.interpretation: This makes the significance of the result legible by anchoring it to both prior tractability and the unresolved boundary.
lessons.application: When presenting a complexity result, explicitly state the nearest known benchmark, the open regime, the exact hardness class, and any condition yielding matching tightness.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the work has no meaningful prior benchmark or when tightness depends on details unavailable in the intended summary.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the formal game input, reduction, complexity assumptions, or the precise meaning of “tight” and “independent adversaries.”
It does not provide quantitative details or conditions for the stationary-point hardness result beyond the stated objective class.
